steps.title: Welcome
steps.summary: OpenCode Workspace Manager keeps your work durable while the runtime stays disposable.
bullets: Workspace means your durable files, notes, history, and outputs.
Runtime means the replaceable Ubuntu tool environment around that work.
Session means the current terminal run inside that runtime.
If the runtime changes, your workspace should still be there.

steps.title: Create a workspace
steps.summary: Start with a name, a folder, and the features you want inside the runtime.
bullets: Choose a clear workspace name. It becomes the visible label in the app.
Keep the suggested folder unless you have a reason to move it.
Workspace files should stay inside the workspace folder so backup and recovery stay simple.
Features and services describe what the runtime should have ready for this workspace.

steps.title: Open a workspace
steps.summary: Select a workspace, then open it from the button or directly from the list.
bullets: Single-click selects a workspace and updates the details panel.
Double-click opens the workspace quickly.
Open Workspace also works from the main action button.
The app validates the runtime and attaches the terminal for you in the background.

steps.title: Work in the terminal
steps.summary: When the terminal opens, you are inside the runtime attached to that workspace.
bullets: Use it like a normal terminal for editing, running tools, and working with code.
Copy and paste works through Windows Terminal.
Open Workspace resumes the latest OpenCode session when one exists. If no OpenCode session exists, a new one is started.

steps.title: Create a Save Point
steps.summary: Save Points are the normal local protection action.
bullets: Create one before a big change.
Create another when the work reaches a good state.
Save Points protect local progress on this machine even if you do not publish yet.

steps.title: Create a Checkpoint
steps.summary: Checkpoints are extra local recovery points when you want stronger local protection.
bullets: A Save Point is your normal progress marker.
A Checkpoint is an additional recovery capture when you want extra safety.
Use it before riskier changes or when you want to preserve more local state.

steps.title: Publish when you want off-machine backup
steps.summary: Publish is for remote backup. It is useful, but it is not required for normal local work.
bullets: Publish sends the current working copy to configured remote backup.
If remote backup is not configured yet, the app should say so clearly.
Local-only work is still valid. Publish is explicit, not automatic.

steps.title: Read the safety panel
steps.summary: The safety panel tells you how well the current workspace is protected.
bullets: Protected means local recovery is in a strong state.
Partially Protected means your work is still safe, but another protection step would help.
Needs Review means the app found something that should be reviewed before publishing.
Needs Review is not the same as lost work. It means stop and check before sending anything remote.

steps.title: Finish with a simple habit
steps.summary: You do not need to learn Docker or Git internals to work safely here.
bullets: Create a Save Point before a big change.
Create another Save Point after a good state.
Publish when you want backup off the machine.
Use the safety panel whenever you are unsure.
